storyboard.claim: We carry other people's tasks because we are desperate for their approval.
storyboard.concreteVisual: The philosopher naming the motive while the youth sags under a load of borrowed tasks.
storyboard.relationToPrevious: Picks up the teetering stack of other people's tasks from the previous beat and names why we grab it.
storyboard.addedInformation: weak: the picture adds only the weighed-down listener; the reason itself is spoken.
storyboard.staging: The philosopher counts off the reason on his fingers while the young man droops under an unseen weight.

storyboard.claim: Adler calls the desire for recognition the master trap of human psychology.
storyboard.concreteVisual: Adler himself stepping forward to name the trap before the example begins.
storyboard.relationToPrevious: Names the trap behind the approval-seeking just described.
storyboard.addedInformation: weak: the frame marks whose diagnosis this is; the trap itself is spoken.
storyboard.staging: Adler lifts one finger: this is the trap people fall into without noticing.

storyboard.claim: Picture the modern corporate climber: alone in a glowing office at midnight, exhausted over a presentation.
storyboard.concreteVisual: One lit desk in a dark office while a clock marks the late hour.
storyboard.relationToPrevious: Cuts from Adler's named trap to the person living inside it.
storyboard.addedInformation: The clock and the dark surroundings make 'midnight, alone, exhausted' readable without sound.
storyboard.staging: The young man slumps over the only bright desk while every cubicle behind him is dark.

storyboard.claim: His personal life is a mess and his friends are gone, but all he wants is tomorrow's pat from the VP.
storyboard.concreteVisual: The trophy of recognition glowing on the dark desk while his own life goes untended.
storyboard.relationToPrevious: Shows what the exhausted climber in the empty office is actually working for.
storyboard.addedInformation: The trophy names the prize as status, and the sad face prices what it costs him.
storyboard.staging: The young man stares hollowly at the trophy: weeks without friends, one line of praise pending.

storyboard.claim: Adlerian psychology smashes this whole scenario of earning recognition.
storyboard.concreteVisual: Adler arriving to demolish the office picture rather than explain it.
storyboard.relationToPrevious: Breaks the scene the last two beats built instead of continuing it.
storyboard.addedInformation: Makes the theory's arrival visible as destruction of the premise, not an addition to it.
storyboard.staging: Adler swings his arm down as if smashing the trophy scene to pieces.

storyboard.claim: The philosopher states it unequivocally: you must deny the desire for recognition.
storyboard.concreteVisual: A target of recognition crossed out the moment the command is given.
storyboard.relationToPrevious: Answers the sledgehammer by naming the exact thing it destroys.
storyboard.addedInformation: The struck target shows the aim itself must be dropped, not only its result.
storyboard.staging: The philosopher cuts his hand across the air: deny this want outright.

storyboard.claim: The youth explodes: no way — recognition is the fundamental universal human drive.
storyboard.concreteVisual: The young man erupting mid-argument, the objection drawn like a blade.
storyboard.relationToPrevious: Rejects the philosopher's command from the previous beat head-on.
storyboard.addedInformation: The sword marks this as a genuine clash, not a polite clarifying question.
storyboard.staging: The young man shoots to his feet and slashes the air with one hand: no way.

storyboard.claim: The philosopher turns the argument into a mechanism: why do we seek recognition at all?
storyboard.concreteVisual: The philosopher pausing the quarrel to examine the machinery behind the want.
storyboard.relationToPrevious: Meets the youth's outburst with the question underneath it.
storyboard.addedInformation: Shifts the frame from assertion to examination so the viewer knows a mechanism is coming.
storyboard.staging: The philosopher tilts his head, hand at his chin: why does anyone want it?

storyboard.claim: Live to satisfy other people's expectations and your life belongs to whoever set them.
storyboard.concreteVisual: The young man hanging limp from another hand's strings, boss, parents and society holding the cross.
storyboard.relationToPrevious: Answers the 'why do we seek it' question with the cost of seeking it.
storyboard.addedInformation: The strings make ownership literal: someone else's hand now moves him.
storyboard.staging: The young man sags in mid-air under a control bar, too tired to fight the strings.

storyboard.claim: Chasing recognition means gauging everyone's feelings, repressing your own desires and living in fear of judgment.
storyboard.concreteVisual: A polite mask held up in front of a face that is tight with dread.
storyboard.relationToPrevious: Details what life under someone else's strings feels like from the inside.
storyboard.addedInformation: The mask shows the repression as a performance worn over fear rather than a mood.
storyboard.staging: The young man holds the smiling mask away from his own worried face, checking it before he wears it.

storyboard.claim: You become a slave to other people's measuring stick, so being disliked is no accidental side effect.
storyboard.concreteVisual: A chain of other people's yardsticks hefted across the speaker's shoulders.
storyboard.relationToPrevious: Names the condition of the masked, string-pulled youth from the last two beats.
storyboard.addedInformation: The chains show the slavery is carried and imposed, not freely chosen.
storyboard.staging: The philosopher hauls the chain up onto one shoulder: enslaved to everyone else's measure.

storyboard.claim: Being disliked is not a unfortunate accident of living your own life — it is the price tag of freedom.
storyboard.concreteVisual: An open door with a scowling young man behind it — the exit that costs their approval.
storyboard.relationToPrevious: Flips the chains of the last beat: what looks like a penalty is the cost of leaving them.
storyboard.addedInformation: The door makes freedom a way out that other people visibly disapprove of.
storyboard.staging: The philosopher points at the open door while the young man glowers behind him at the choice.

storyboard.claim: The book adds a theological angle — God and nihilism — to explain why this trap is everywhere today.
storyboard.concreteVisual: The philosopher opening a new thread of the argument, hands spread wide.
storyboard.relationToPrevious: Widens the trap from one person's office to an entire era's belief structure.
storyboard.addedInformation: weak: the frame only marks the topic change; the theology arrives in the audio.
storyboard.staging: The philosopher spreads both hands: the argument now reaches beyond psychology.

storyboard.claim: In religious societies recognition was aimed upward at God, so the neighbors' approval was not strictly needed.
storyboard.concreteVisual: The philosopher pointing up at the old divine audience that used to do the watching.
storyboard.relationToPrevious: Supplies the historical half of the God-and-nihilism angle just introduced.
storyboard.addedInformation: The upward gesture shows where judgment used to come from and who was already pleased.
storyboard.staging: The philosopher lifts his eyes and one finger heavenward: the old gaze ran upward.

storyboard.claim: In a secular modern world where many have dropped God, a massive psychological void opens up.
storyboard.concreteVisual: The philosopher holding his hands around empty air where the old audience used to be.
storyboard.relationToPrevious: States the consequence of the secular shift the previous beat described.
storyboard.addedInformation: Makes the void a visible absence instead of an abstract term.
storyboard.staging: The philosopher shapes an empty gap in front of his chest: something used to sit there.

storyboard.claim: With no one watching from above, we substitute society's recognition to fill the god-shaped hole.
storyboard.concreteVisual: A two-step flow: god-shaped hole -> society's recognition.
storyboard.relationToPrevious: Turns the stated void into the substitution people make to close it.
storyboard.addedInformation: Shows the swap as cause and effect: the hole is what gets filled.
storyboard.staging: The philosopher gestures from the empty gap outward to the crowd: that is what replaces it.

storyboard.claim: We demand that bosses and Instagram followers validate our existence — and Adler says deny that need entirely.
storyboard.concreteVisual: A phone stacked with follower likes, which Adler indicates and then refuses.
storyboard.relationToPrevious: Names what society's recognition looks like on a screen in the present day.
storyboard.addedInformation: The phone dates the hunger: followers now supply the approval the divine used to supply.
storyboard.staging: Adler points at the glowing wall of likes, then cuts it away with one flat hand.

callout.text: find our worth without anyone else

storyboard.claim: We must find our worth without anyone else to validate it — and the youth immediately pushes the claim to its limit.
storyboard.concreteVisual: The philosopher holding the self-sufficient ideal out while the young man leans in to break it.
storyboard.onScreenText: find our worth without anyone else
storyboard.relationToPrevious: Gives the answer to the validation hunger shown on the phone.
storyboard.addedInformation: The youth's forward lean signals the coming objection before he voices it.
storyboard.staging: The philosopher offers the idea with an open palm; the young man is already coiled to test it.

storyboard.claim: If I totally stop caring what people think, don't I just become a tyrant?
storyboard.concreteVisual: The young man pressing the objection: total indifference must produce a monster.
storyboard.relationToPrevious: Takes the self-worth prescription of the last beat to its logical extreme.
storyboard.addedInformation: Frames the objection as a moral danger rather than a technical quibble.
storyboard.staging: The young man leans in, palm upturned: doesn't that turn me into a tyrant?

storyboard.claim: His example of the tyrant: King Lear, or a modern billionaire dictator who destroys everything for his own whims.
storyboard.concreteVisual: The youth sweeping an invisible table clean as he impersonates the self-centered despot.
storyboard.relationToPrevious: Gives the tyrant raised in the last beat a recognizable face.
storyboard.addedInformation: Updates Lear into a current image so the objection lands without a literature lesson.
storyboard.staging: The young man rears up impersonating a raging strongman, arm sweeping everything aside.

callout.text: aren't I just giving myself permission

storyboard.claim: Not caring whether people dislike me sounds like handing myself philosophical permission to be awful.
storyboard.concreteVisual: The young man staring at his own open palm — permission he would be granting himself.
storyboard.onScreenText: aren't I just giving myself permission
storyboard.relationToPrevious: Sharpens the tyrant worry of the earlier beats into its underlying logic.
storyboard.addedInformation: The key makes permission something he hands himself rather than receives from anyone.
storyboard.staging: The young man stares at the key in his hand, uneasy about what it unlocks.

storyboard.claim: The twist: obsessing over how others see you is actually the most self-centered way to live.
storyboard.concreteVisual: The philosopher turning one hand over the other, flipping the premise while the youth freezes.
storyboard.relationToPrevious: Answers the permission worry by reversing who is really the selfish one.
storyboard.addedInformation: Marks the reversal as the pivot so the viewer knows the argument has turned around.
storyboard.staging: The philosopher rotates his open hand over and the whole argument inside out.

storyboard.claim: The youth objects: how can trying to please people possibly be self-centered, when you are doing things for them?
storyboard.concreteVisual: The young man cutting in with the obvious objection, brows up, hands spread.
storyboard.relationToPrevious: Voices the confusion the twist just created in the previous beat.
storyboard.addedInformation: weak: the frame only stages the objection; the reasoning arrives in the audio.
storyboard.staging: The young man throws both hands up: I am literally doing things for them.

storyboard.claim: You appear to be looking at other people, but you are actually only looking at yourself.
storyboard.concreteVisual: The philosopher tracing the youth's outward gaze away and then straight back into his own chest.
storyboard.relationToPrevious: Explains the self-centeredness the youth doubted in the last beat.
storyboard.addedInformation: Makes the reversal spatial: the looking-out was always looking-in.
storyboard.staging: The philosopher's finger travels from the young man's eyes out to the room and back to himself.

storyboard.claim: Other people become mirrors that reflect only your own worth back at you.
storyboard.concreteVisual: A mirror held up where the boss should be — others reduced to reflection.
storyboard.relationToPrevious: Names the mechanism behind the self-directed looking described in the previous beat.
storyboard.addedInformation: The mirror shows others have become props for self-assessment instead of people.
storyboard.staging: The young man holds a mirror toward the room and looks into it instead of at anyone.

storyboard.claim: You don't care about the boss; you care about the boss's opinion of you.
storyboard.concreteVisual: A mask angled at the boss's chair — the performance matters, the person does not.
storyboard.relationToPrevious: Applies the mirror point to the concrete case of the boss.
storyboard.addedInformation: The mask shows the relationship runs through performance rather than through the other person.
storyboard.staging: The young man talks past the empty chair, adjusting his face for the verdict instead of the man.

storyboard.claim: The tyrant who forces his will and the people-pleaser who twists herself into knots are both fundamentally self-centered.
storyboard.concreteVisual: The two men side by side — one pushing out, one folding in — under a single verdict.
storyboard.relationToPrevious: Merges the tyrant of the earlier beats with the people-pleaser just shown.
storyboard.addedInformation: Delivers the reversal's punchline: opposite behaviors, identical obsession with the self.
storyboard.staging: The philosopher sets one hand high and one low, then brings them level: the same thing.

storyboard.claim: True freedom is asking whose task it is to like me — theirs — and handing it back.
storyboard.concreteVisual: The philosopher lifting the question off his own chest and holding it out to be returned.
storyboard.relationToPrevious: Applies the book's separation-of-tasks test to the approval just discussed.
storyboard.addedInformation: The hand-back gesture turns the remedy into an action instead of a feeling.
storyboard.staging: The philosopher mimes picking something off his own chest and offering it to the young man.

storyboard.claim: Focus on what you can contribute to them, not on whether they applaud you for it.
storyboard.concreteVisual: A gift offered forward — contribution given for its own sake, with no applause attached.
storyboard.relationToPrevious: Replaces the handed-back task of the last beat with what is actually yours to give.
storyboard.addedInformation: The gift flips the direction of the exchange: outward giving instead of inward collecting.
storyboard.staging: The philosopher holds the gift out with both hands, expecting nothing back in return.

storyboard.claim: If we are not supposed to seek applause, we must rethink how we give it — the subject becomes praise.
storyboard.concreteVisual: The argument turning outward: the philosopher's open palm now aimed at handing praise out.
storyboard.relationToPrevious: Pivots from the applause we seek to the applause we give.
storyboard.addedInformation: Marks the chapter turn so the viewer knows the critique now targets the giver.
storyboard.staging: The philosopher turns his palm outward: now this question belongs to us.

storyboard.claim: This may be the most counterintuitive part of the whole framework — especially for a parent, teacher or manager.
storyboard.concreteVisual: The young man taken aback, hand at his chin, bracing before the example opens.
storyboard.relationToPrevious: Warns that the praise rethink will feel wrong to anyone who supervises others.
storyboard.addedInformation: Names the audience this will hit — parents, teachers, managers — before the scene begins.
storyboard.staging: The young man blinks and leans back: the warning lands before the example does.

storyboard.claim: The scene: a mother and her young child, who has just helped set the dinner table.
storyboard.concreteVisual: A dinner plate on the family table as the child carries a cup into place.
storyboard.relationToPrevious: Paints the domestic example on which the praise argument will be tested.
storyboard.addedInformation: Puts the claim in a real kitchen so the critique lands on something familiar.
storyboard.staging: The young man carries a cup to the set table, pleased with his own help.

storyboard.claim: The mother pats the child's head and sings 'such a good helper' — and would never do that for her husband doing the same job.
storyboard.concreteVisual: A hand coming down onto an upturned head while the praiser beams in a raised voice.
storyboard.relationToPrevious: Follows the child's help from the last beat with the praise it earns.
storyboard.addedInformation: The downward hand and the sing-song quote make the tone visible: praise descends from above.
storyboard.staging: The philosopher reaches down to pat an upturned head, face beaming; the young man below takes it.

storyboard.claim: With her husband she only says thank you — and the tone of voice still carries a subtle hidden hierarchy.
storyboard.concreteVisual: The same two now level, an even look exchanged — no hand comes down this time.
storyboard.relationToPrevious: Contrasts the adult thank-you with the child's head-pat of the previous beat.
storyboard.addedInformation: The level gaze beside the earlier downward pat exposes the ranking without needing the audio.
storyboard.staging: The two men stand level and exchange a plain thank-you, eyes straight across.

storyboard.claim: Adler's quiet, devastating claim: praise is inherently toxic because it comes from a vertical relationship.
storyboard.concreteVisual: A ladder between two levels — praise passed down from above, never across.
storyboard.relationToPrevious: Names the hidden hierarchy the kitchen scene just exposed.
storyboard.addedInformation: The ladder shows praise as a downward transaction instead of a warm exchange.
storyboard.staging: Adler indicates the rung above and the rung below: praise only travels one direction.

storyboard.claim: Praise is judgment passed from someone of supposed ability and authority down to someone of no ability — she is above the child.
storyboard.concreteVisual: The philosopher standing a head taller, palm held high over the young man's head.
storyboard.relationToPrevious: Shows who occupies which rung of the ladder just drawn.
storyboard.addedInformation: Makes the vertical relationship physical: one hand speaks down, the other can only receive.
storyboard.staging: The philosopher holds a flat palm above the young man's head: judgment is issued from up here.

storyboard.claim: She judges the child's action against her own yardstick of what is good — and the book compares it to animal training.
storyboard.concreteVisual: The philosopher delivering the book's bluntest comparison without softening it.
storyboard.relationToPrevious: Escalates the judgment critique into the book's harshest analogy.
storyboard.addedInformation: The analogy reframes praise as behavioral control rather than encouragement.
storyboard.staging: The philosopher lowers his hand and says it flat: this is training, not respect.

storyboard.claim: Giving a dog a treat for sitting is not respect for its autonomy — it is a reward for compliance.
storyboard.concreteVisual: The treat held up where the dog must look to earn it.
storyboard.relationToPrevious: Supplies the concrete example of the animal-training comparison just made.
storyboard.addedInformation: The raised treat shows the reward steering the behavior instead of respecting a choice.
storyboard.staging: The young man lifts the treat high; the dog sits and follows it upward.

storyboard.claim: Reward and punishment education — how the entire school system and corporate HR operate — is just the carrot and the stick.
storyboard.concreteVisual: A school standing over the exchange: rewards and penalties handed out at scale.
storyboard.relationToPrevious: Extends the single dog treat of the last beat to whole institutions.
storyboard.addedInformation: The school icon scales the trick from one animal to an entire system.
storyboard.staging: The philosopher points at the school: this is where the carrot and the stick are issued.

storyboard.claim: Grading people and praising them trains people pleasers who only act to get the carrot.
storyboard.concreteVisual: A two-step flow: praising them -> people pleasers.
storyboard.relationToPrevious: Shows the result of the carrot-and-stick system named in the previous beat.
storyboard.addedInformation: Turns the accusation into a causal chain: the training produces the personality.
storyboard.staging: The philosopher traces the chain from the raised reward across to the waiting people-pleaser.
